fixes.explanation: No waiting happens here. The text says Ahimaaz "ran by way of the plain and outran the Cushite." The Cushite had taken off first, so Ahimaaz is the one who ends up ahead. Waiting for him would have meant staying behind, and that's not what Ahimaaz does.
It's true. The watchman says the first man appears to be running like Ahimaaz son of Zadok. The king answers, "This is a good man." Then he adds, "He comes with good news."
It's true. "…the king covered his face and cried out at the top of his voice…" the text says. The people had already slipped back into the city quietly before this. David is still grieving his son.
The text says the people were told, "Behold, the king is sitting in the gate." Then "…they all came before the king." David has gotten up as Joab urged. Joab had told him, "Now therefore get up!"

It's true. The people were told, "Behold, the king is sitting in the gate." And "…they all came before the king." Joab had told David, "Go out and speak comfort to your servants…" Now the king is out where his men can see him.

Joab never says that. His reason is that "…the king’s son is dead." Joab then sends a Cushite to tell the king what he has seen, so the fighting is not what holds Ahimaaz back. Today is just not the day for Ahimaaz to carry good news.

Not quite. Joab tells a Cushite, "Go, tell the king what you have seen." Joab's reason for holding Ahimaaz back is different: "…because the king’s son is dead." He says Ahimaaz may carry good news another day, just not today.

Right, he does not drop it. Ahimaaz "persisted," and he asks Joab, "No matter what, please let me also run behind the Cushite!" Joab asks why he wants to run when he will not receive a reward. Ahimaaz answers, "No matter what, I want to run!"
Joab says, "Then run!" Ahimaaz had said, "No matter what, I want to run!" and Joab lets him go. Joab had asked why he wanted to run with no reward coming, and Ahimaaz held firm.
Joab doesn't send him back to the troops. After Ahimaaz insists, Joab tells him, "Then run!" So Ahimaaz is cleared to run behind the Cushite, just as he asked.

The text says Ahimaaz "ran by way of the plain and outran the Cushite." The Cushite had set out first, and Ahimaaz still ended up ahead of him. Starting behind and finishing in front is a good feeling, friend.
It's the other way around. The Cushite took off first, but Ahimaaz "ran by way of the plain and outran the Cushite." Ahimaaz is the one who ends up ahead.
David says, "If he is alone, he bears good news." The watchman sees a man running alone and calls out to tell the king. To David, a lone runner points to good news.

David doesn't say enemies are coming. When the watchman reports the runner, the king answers, "If he is alone, he bears good news." Then another man appears, and David says, "This one also brings good news," so he reads both runners the same way.

David asks, "Is the young man Absalom all right?" Absalom is David's son, the one who had been declared king in Hebron against him (2 Samuel 15:10). Ahimaaz brought news of victory, and the king asks about his son first. I think that tells you where his heart is.

The forest is where the battle was fought (2 Samuel 18:6), and David isn't there. The text says he "…went up to the chamber over the gate and wept." He weeps right by the gate where he waited for news.
David cries, "If only I had died instead of you, O Absalom, my son, my son!" This is a father's grief, and it's heavy. In the same breath he calls out "my son, my son!"
Nothing about fleeing comes out of David's mouth here. What he wishes is that he had died instead of his son. His words are, "If only I had died instead of you, O Absalom, my son, my son!"
Fear is not the word the text uses. The word is mourning, and the people were told, "The king is grieving over his son." Then they "returned to the city quietly that day…"

Joab never brings up fear. His charge is about love and hate, and it goes on: "I know today that if Absalom were alive and all of us were dead, it would have pleased you!" Those are Joab's words, spoken to the king in his house.
